questions.q: What is the real cost of setting OWD to Public Read/Write 'to avoid sharing rules later,' per this lesson?
options: Nothing stays private by default, so future access control has to be bolted on with restriction rules instead of designed in
There is no real cost — it's a safe shortcut
It makes the org-wide default impossible to change later
It automatically disables all permission sets
questions.explain: The lesson frames this as deferred, larger cost: more total work later, done in the wrong order, because nothing was private to begin with.

questions.q: Why is granting View All or Modify All 'just to unblock' a user risky, according to this lesson?
options: It has no risk as long as it's documented
It only affects field-level security, not records
It bypasses restriction rules and sharing entirely, and is often never narrowed back down once the ticket closes
It automatically expires after 30 days
questions.explain: View All/Modify All override the narrowing tools from Lesson 16, and the lesson notes the 'narrow it later' intention frequently never happens.

questions.q: What is 'profile explosion,' as described in this lesson?
options: A security vulnerability in the profile object
A limit on the number of profiles an org can have
An error that occurs when two profiles conflict
Creating many near-identical cloned profiles instead of one base profile plus permission sets for variations
questions.explain: Profile explosion happens when profiles are cloned for every job variation instead of using permission sets to layer on the differences, creating many profiles that must be maintained independently.

questions.q: According to the lesson, when sharing rules keep multiplying to cover most of an org, what should that signal to an admin?
options: That more sharing rules should be added to finish the job
That it may be time to revisit whether the underlying OWD choice is actually right
That the role hierarchy should be deleted
That restriction rules are no longer needed
questions.explain: The lesson treats heavy sharing-rule stacking as a sign the OWD itself should be reconsidered, rather than continuing to patch around it.

questions.q: What is the common pattern the lesson identifies across all five mistakes?
options: Each mistake is a locally reasonable shortcut under time pressure that defers cost onto whoever maintains the org later
Each mistake stems from not knowing the available tools
Each mistake only happens in Developer Edition orgs
Each mistake is caused by a Salesforce platform bug
questions.explain: The lesson's closing point is that these aren't knowledge gaps — they're the fast tool chosen over the right one, with the cost deferred rather than avoided.
